question: Explain how the interference fringes are formed.
markScheme:
As the waves pass through the two narrow slits, they diffract (spread out) which allows waves from each slit to overlap and superpose

waves from the double slit are coherent (meaning they have constant phase difference over time)

depending on question context, the answer proceeds as follows:

(A) source are in phase

Constructive interference (Maxima / Bright Fringe/ Loud sound) occurs at points where the path difference is nλ (n = 0,1,2,3…) the waves superpose in phase to interfere constructively.

Destructive interference (Minima / Dark fringe / Soft sound) occurs at points where the path difference is (n + ½)λ (n = 0,1,2,3…) the waves superpose in anti-phase to interfere destructively

(B) source are in anti phase (not tested often)

Constructive interference (Maxima / Bright Fringe/ Loud sound) occurs at points where the path difference is (n + ½)λ (n = 0,1,2,3…) the waves superpose in phase to interfere constructively.

Destructive interference (Minima / Dark fringe / Soft sound) occurs at points where the path difference is nλ (n = 0,1,2,3…) the waves superpose in anti-phase to interfere destructively

BONUS:
If asked for “observable interference pattern” include:

The two superposing waves should have equal or roughly equal amplitude.

question: State the conditions required for maxima to be formed in an interference pattern produced by two sources of microwaves.
markScheme:
Two waves must overlap and superpose

both sources are coherent / have constant phase difference (not just constant λ or frequency)

waves meet/ superpose in phase at that point to interfere constructively (phase difference when they superpose = 0, 2π, 4π… 2nπ or path difference = 0, λ, 2λ if sources are in phase)

same direction of polarisation or unpolarised

markScheme:

waves reach in phase or phase difference = 0, 2π, 4π… 2nπ

constructive interference, hence it is an intensity maximum

question: Explain why the pattern of fringes on the screen is seen over a limited area of the screen.
markScheme:
As light passes through the two narrow slits, it diffracts (spread out) allowing the two beams to overlap and superpose

The resulting double slit interference pattern of constant fringe separation is enveloped / modulated by the single slit diffraction pattern of the individual slits.

The intensity of diffracted light from each slit decreases from the central maximum to zero at the first single slit diffraction minimum

Therefore, interference fringes are only bright and visible within this central single slit maximum, limiting the pattern to a small central area of the screen,

path difference of exactly 1 λ such that

waves reach with a phase difference of 360° / 2π

(by principal of superposition) waves interfere constructively to produce the first order maxima

question: Suggest one reason why the fringe pattern produced by light passing through a diffraction grating is brighter than that produced from the same source with a double slit.
markScheme: More slits for light to pass through such that bright fringe comprise light from more sources superposing in phase to give a higher peak intensity.

question: State the conditions required for the formation of a standing wave/stationary wave.
markScheme:
two waves travelling in opposite directions (along the same straight line) superposing

waves are same type and have same speed, frequency and wavelength (and approximately equal amplitudes for complete cancellation at nodes)

Note: coherence is NOT accepted here. (coherence is a source relationship for 2D interference e.g. double slit type of interference. Standing waves meet with different phase differences depending on the point at which they meet e.g. meet in antiphase at node, in phase at antinode)

question: Use the principle of superposition to explain the formation of a standing / stationary wave.
markScheme:
Two progressive waves of the same type, speed, and frequency travel in opposite directions along the same straight line

As the waves overlap, they superpose such that the resultant displacement at any point is the vector sum of their individual displacements

At points where they arrive constantly in phase, they constructively superpose to form antinodes (points of maximum amplitude). At points where they arrive constantly in anti-phase, they cancel out to form nodes (points of zero amplitude)

question: Explain how the standing / stationary wave is formed on a string attached to a wall.
markScheme:
Progressive transverse wave moves along string and reflects at fixed point/end/wall/boundary (producing a reflected progressive wave travelling in opposite direction)

the incident and reflected waves have the same speed, frequency and wavelength

They superpose such that at points where they arrive constantly in phase, they constructively superpose to form antinodes and at points where they arrive in anti-phase, they destructively interfere to form nodes.

question:
An incident sinusoidal sound wave of a single frequency travels up a tube.

Explain how the standing / stationary wave is formed from the incident sound wave.
markScheme:
The incident progressive sound wave travels up the tube and reflects off the end of the tube (either the open or closed boundary), producing a reflected progressive wave travelling in the opposite direction

The incident and reflected sound waves have the same speed, frequency, and wavelength (as they originate from the same source and travel through the same medium inside the tube)

The waves overlap and superpose inside the tube. Points of constant in-phase superposition form antinodes (maximum amplitude), and points of constant anti-phase superposition form nodes (zero amplitude)

question:
A microwave detector is placed between a source of microwaves S and a metal reflector R.

Describe how standing /stationary waves are formed between R and S.
markScheme:
microwave from source S reflects at reflector R

The incident and reflected waves travel in opposite directions with the same speed, frequency, and wavelength (as they originate from the same source)

The two waves meet and superpose. At points where they arrive constantly in phase, they constructively superpose to form antinodes (maximum intensity). At points where they arrive constant in antiphase, they destructively superpose to form nodes.

question: State the features of a standing /stationary wave that distinguish it from a progressive wave.

no net energy transfer (progressive transfer energy in direction of wave propagation)

amplitude varies along its length (progressive: all particles oscillate with same amplitude)

nodes and antinodes (progressive don’t have)

neighbouring points within inter-nodal loop vibrate in phase (progressive wave particles have varying phases)

question:

markScheme:

While the standing wave profile does not advance (no energy transfer), speed refers to the speed of incident and reflected progressive waves
